item.title: ‘Flashing light’ that saved six
item.description: AFTER nearly 37 hours adrift at sea with nothing but life jackets and a wooden plank to keep them afloat, the six medical workers from Lau were running out of hope. But as darkness surrounded them, a mysterious flashlight appeared in the distance, a small beam that would eventually guide rescuers to their location.
item.content:encoded:
AFTER nearly 37 hours adrift at sea with nothing but life jackets and a wooden plank to keep them afloat, the six medical workers from Lau were running out of hope.

But as darkness surrounded them, a mysterious flashlight appeared in the distance, a small beam that would eventually guide rescuers to their location.

A faint flashlight beam, impossible to explain given the distance and the rough conditions, pierced through the night, guiding the crew of the Lomaiviti Princess XII towards the missing medical team and ending one of the most intense maritime searches in recent memory.

For Captain Adriano Rabolabiu, the moment was nothing short of divine intervention. Mr Rabolabiu recalled receiving the distressing news that a boat carrying seven people had capsized while travelling in Lau waters, as they were travelling to Vanuavatu in Lau.

His immediate concern was reaching the missing medical workers as quickly as possible. The search began with a series of urgent calls. Mr Rabolabiu said he contacted Lakeba Hospital and was told the medical team had departed after 8pm but had not arrived at their destination by midnight.

He then began checking whether nearby vessels and authorities had been informed.

“There’s a vessel just ahead of us. Have you informed them that they are missing people out at sea?” he recalled asking.

After being told only police had been notified, Mr Rabolabiu said he immediately took action. He contacted the vessel ahead, informed the Republic of Fiji Military Forces, and requested regular updates while the search continued.

The next morning, a message from the Navy appeared to bring relief.

“At 10 o’clock in the morning, he (a crew mate) came running to me. He said, there’s a text from the Navy. They’ve been found in Nayau.”

He rushed to the wheelhouse and checked the message himself. However, as he began making further calls, he realised something was wrong.

The information was later confirmed to be false after a vessel searching the area had been mistaken for the missing boat.

The search continued. Mr Rabolabiu contacted communities across Lau, including Oneata, Olorua and Komo, asking whether anyone had seen signs of the missing team.

Still, there was no news. After reaching Vanuavatu in Lau and unloading passengers and supplies, the captain decided the search would continue.

“We just had the passengers disembark with all their shopping things and their essential items they need for two weeks.

“The building material and the big drums, we left it on board and we took off. Because we were losing daylight.”

He said maritime law requires a ship captain to assist people in distress. At around 3pm, Mr Rabolabiu gathered his crew in the wheelhouse and began coordinating a wider search.

“I then announced to the passengers to help us look. Everyone helped us. They were shining lights because it would reflect on the teams life jackets, for us to spot.”

As the ship moved through the waters searching for any sign of the missing medical workers, Mr Rabolabiu went inside to pray.

“I have a prayer called Divine Mercy — ‘Jesus, I trust in you’. It never failed me and it didn’t fail me.”

Then came the moment that changed the search. From above the vessel, crew members began shouting.

“Light, light, light!” The crew had spotted a flashing light in the darkness.

Mr Rabolabiu immediately contacted Lakeba Hospital to confirm whether the missing team had a flashlight.

“They said no, they had nothing but life jackets and a plank,” he said. For the captain, the circumstances surrounding the light were difficult to explain.

After the rescue, he calculated the distance between where the light was spotted and where the survivors were found.

“It was 2.6 nautical miles. As a ship captain, that was a very unlikely odd. Imagine a torchlight at 2.6 miles, shining through waves like that (rough mounting waves).

“When we came close, right to the end when they were just about 100 metres away, I still couldn’t see them properly because of the waves. But the guys on top could see them.”

It was later learnt that as the crew while out at sea prayed for as long as they can and out of the blue a Toshiba flash light floated towards them allowing them ship and signal at the vessel later.

The rescue operation began at about 7pm. However, getting the exhausted medical workers safely aboard was another challenge.

Mr Rabolabiu said the crew had difficulty deploying the rescue dinghy due to the rough conditions. But eventually, the team was brought safely aboard.

item.title: Rescue shows frontline dedication
item.description: THE rescue of six health workers from Lau waters has highlighted the need to support not only health infrastructure but also the people and systems delivering medical services. Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the incident underscored the dedication of health workers serving communities, particularly in remote areas.
item.content:encoded:
THE rescue of six health workers from Lau waters has highlighted the need to support not only health infrastructure but also the people and systems delivering medical services.

Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the incident underscored the dedication of health workers serving communities, particularly in remote areas.

He said while Australia was working with the Fijian Government to support future health infrastructure, including planning for the redevelopment of the Colonial War Memorial Hospital, effective health services depended on more than buildings.

“At this stage, we’ve supported work on what’s called the clinical services plan,” he said.

“So we have an assessment of what’s actually needed and then on the master plan for what comes after CWM.”

Mr Roberts said the Fijian Government was considering the next steps and Australia remained interested in supporting the project.

“It’s a big project, so I think you’ll probably have lots of people working with you on CWM, but it’s really important.”

“We’ll work on the infrastructure, but we’ll also work with the ministry to support the wraparound of all that.”

He described the rescue of the Lau health workers as “fantastic”, saying it highlighted the importance of frontline workers alongside infrastructure investment.

Mr Roberts said Australia remained keen to support the CWMH project as discussions progressed, noting a development of that scale would require multiple partners

item.title: People First claims FijiFirst political legacy
item.description: THE People First party has officially identified itself as the political successor to the deregistered FijiFirst Party. Speaking at the party launch last Saturday, leader Inia Seruiratu said the party was formed after the deregistration of FijiFirst in July 2023, arguing that the move left thousands of supporters without their chosen political representation.
item.content:encoded:
THE People First party has officially identified itself as the political successor to the deregistered FijiFirst Party.

Speaking at the party launch last Saturday, leader Inia Seruiratu said the party was formed after the deregistration of FijiFirst in July 2023, arguing that the move left thousands of supporters without their chosen political representation.

Mr Seruiratu said former FijiFirst members who remained in Parliament as independents had the freedom to choose their own political paths but decided to remain committed to those who had voted them into office.

“During that critical period, we faced immense pressure, but we stood our ground because of you that voted us in,” he said.

“We refused to compromise the faith you placed in us. We chose to stand firm for Fijians who believe in equality, integrity, respect, and national unity.”

He said those circumstances led to the creation of People First.

Mr Seruiratu also said the party would not release a manifesto before consulting the public, saying community input would shape its policy platform.

He also criticised the current state of governance, saying promises of improved transparency, accountability and higher standards had not been fulfilled.

Mr Seruiratu said People First aimed to offer an alternative built on constitutional principles and a commitment to honesty and collaboration with the public.

item.title: CCTV network expands
item.description: THE Government is investing in a nationwide CCTV camera project as part of its expanding communications infrastructure, says Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua. Mr Naivalurua made the comments while officiating at the Pacific Fiber Conference at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa in Nadi last week.
item.content:encoded:
THE Government is investing in a nationwide CCTV camera project as part of its expanding communications infrastructure, says Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua.

Mr Naivalurua made the comments while officiating at the Pacific Fiber Conference at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa in Nadi last week.

“This initiative has already taken shape in the Central Division and will be progressively expanded across the country,” he said.

“Additionally, we are also investing in advanced technologies to bolster our fight against drugs and other serious crimes, ensuring our law enforcement agencies have the tools necessary to keep our communities safe and secure.”

Mr Naivalurua said digital transformation could only succeed if every Fijian was able to participate.

“While market investment continues to expand connectivity across our country, the Government remains committed to ensuring that rural, remote and maritime communities are not left behind.

“Through the universal service scheme administered by the Telecommunications Authority of Fiji, or TAF, we continue to extend telecommunication services to communities where commercial deployment alone is not economically viable.”

Mr Naivalurua said more than 54 universal service sites had been commissioned, with implementation continuing nationwide.

He said phase two was under development and would target another 113 communities.

item.title: inDepth I The sugar dilemma – Call for new direction as industry faces challenges
item.description: THE sugar industry is draining Fiji’s economy, and the country can no longer afford to continue supporting it in its current form, says People’s Alliance party (PA) president Ratu Josefa Dimuri. Ratu Josefa believes major changes are needed, including considering private management of the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), closing the mills on Viti Levu and making Labasa the main centre for sugar produ
item.content:encoded:
THE sugar industry is draining Fiji’s economy, and the country can no longer afford to continue supporting it in its current form, says People’s Alliance party (PA) president Ratu Josefa Dimuri.

Ratu Josefa believes major changes are needed, including considering private management of the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), closing the mills on Viti Levu and making Labasa the main centre for sugar production.

“I do not think we can afford to continue depending on this crop for much longer. It is draining the economy rather than contributing to the economy,” he said.

Ratu Josefa said sugar used to be one of Fiji’s biggest contributors to the economy but that was no longer the case.

“It has now become one of the biggest drains on the economy.”

His comments come as Government continues to invest millions of dollars into the industry while facing problems with cane supply, ageing mills, labour shortages and rising costs.

Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna has acknowledged that Government was investing significant money into the sector while returns remained a concern.

Mr Tunabuna had also confirmed Government was paying about $18million each year to service debts, including money owed to the Exim Bank of India.

Ratu Josefa said the situation could not continue.

“I believe it is time to make that shift. We have to make that shift because we cannot afford to wait any longer.”

He suggested that the Government consider closing the mills on Viti Levu and concentrating sugar production in Labasa.

“I would like to suggest that we close the mills in Viti Levu and only concentrate sugar production at Labasa. We should improve the quality of the crop and increase production there.”

But the proposal comes at a difficult time for the Labasa mill.

The mill stopped crushing during the first three weeks of the current crushing season because of low or no cane supply.

No mill breakdowns were recorded during that period.

Mr Tunabuna said the start of the crushing season had been difficult because of the fuel crisis and other disruptions.

“It’s not a normal year. It has been a very difficult year for us to start with one with the fuel crisis, and second with some interferences along the way,” he said.

Despite the difficulties, Mr Tunabuna praised Northern farmers for continuing to harvest and deliver cane.

“I am particularly happy about the farming community here in the North for their perseverance and how resilient they are in carrying out required tasks towards harvesting.”

Farmers had signed the Master Award Growers Agreement and decided to continue harvesting.

“They decided for themselves that they would have to continue, and they did exactly that.”

The Labasa mill needs between 5500 and 6000 tonnes of cane each day to keep operating.

However, it has been receiving only about 3500 to 4000 tonnes. The shortage means the mill cannot operate at its full capacity.

Fiji’s aging sugar mills is another major concern.

Mr Tunabuna said the mills needed regular maintenance because of their age and defended the practice of closing mills on Sundays.

“Closing on Sundays for repair and maintenance work is very normal. It gives time for some maintenance to be done for the mills.”

“This has been the practice simply because our mills are very old mills. We simply cannot wait until we have a big breakdown.”

He said it was also not practical to keep crushing when there was very little cane available.

“It also coincides when there is a very low supply of cane on Sundays. So it is not a very good idea to be crushing when you won’t have the cane.”

Mr Tunabuna said stopping the mill allowed maintenance workers to carry out checks and repairs before more cane arrived.

item.title: Young voice takes carnival crown
item.description: YEAR 12 student Mere Mafi Sigavunau was overcome with surprise and tears of joy after being crowned Miss FMF Duavata 2026 at Subrail Park in Labasa. Ms Sigavunau, who represented Security Shield Services, received the crown during the closing of the FMF Duavata Northern Crime Prevention Carnival on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
YEAR 12 student Mere Mafi Sigavunau was overcome with surprise and tears of joy after being crowned Miss FMF Duavata 2026 at Subrail Park in Labasa.

Ms Sigavunau, who represented Security Shield Services, received the crown during the closing of the FMF Duavata Northern Crime Prevention Carnival on Saturday.

The emotional moment followed a week of advocacy, with contestants raising awareness about issues affecting communities, including drugs and substance abuse.

She thanked her fellow contestants for their support and for sharing the journey with her throughout the carnival.

“I also want to thank my fellow contestants. It has been a great pleasure to stand with you, and it has been quite a journey to share with you,” she said.

Ms Sigavunau acknowledged her parents and friends for their “endless love, support and encouragement”.

She also recognised her cousin, Josh, for supporting her throughout the competition.

She said winning the crown was a privilege and promised to carry the title with pride.

“Being crowned tonight has been a pleasure, and I promise to wear this crown with humility and dignity.”

The carnival concluded after a week of advocacy, competitions and community activities aimed at promoting crime prevention.

item.title: Accused challenges police interview
item.description: A TERTIARY student charged with the manslaughter of Jone Vuinakelo has filed an application for a voir dire challenging the admissibility of his police interview. Defence lawyer Kalisito Maisamoa, representing Aisake Lovobalavu, confirmed this to Justice Pita Bulamainaivalu in the High Court in Suva last month.
item.content:encoded:
A TERTIARY student charged with the manslaughter of Jone Vuinakelo has filed an application for a voir dire challenging the admissibility of his police interview.

Defence lawyer Kalisito Maisamoa, representing Aisake Lovobalavu, confirmed this to Justice Pita Bulamainaivalu in the High Court in Suva last month.

Mr Lovobalavu faces one count of manslaughter.

Police allege that Mr Vuinakelo, 30, was found with severe facial injuries at Nauluvatu settlement in Suva on March 15.

At the previous court sitting, Mr Maisamoa submitted that the interview was conducted immediately after a drinking session and that his client was intoxicated during prolonged police questioning.

He further alleged that parts of the interview transcript appeared to contain answers induced by police.

To support the challenge, the defence has requested disclosure of the full video recording of the interview, which has yet to be provided by the State.

The State has served the victim’s post-mortem and toxicology reports on the defence.

item.title: Market may feature annually
item.description: THE People’s Alliance party Youth Wing has committed to making its “Youth Skills Market” an annual event as it looks to create more opportunities for young entrepreneurs and connect youth with business and employment pathways. Speaking at the market, Youth Wing general secretary Kava Masilagi said the initiative was designed as a youth-focused fair and night market where young entrepreneurs and lo
item.content:encoded:
THE People’s Alliance party Youth Wing has committed to making its “Youth Skills Market” an annual event as it looks to create more opportunities for young entrepreneurs and connect youth with business and employment pathways.

Speaking at the market, Youth Wing general secretary Kava Masilagi said the initiative was designed as a youth-focused fair and night market where young entrepreneurs and local businesses could showcase their products and services.

She said the event brought together young vendors, including a 17-year-old selling homemade flower foams and slides, while also providing space for businesses to engage with potential young employees through recruitment activities.

“We’ve just really tried to make this a youth-friendly space, where youth can access other youth entrepreneurs,” Ms Masilagi said.

“And not only interact with them but also gain some encouragement.”

The market also served as a platform for employment opportunities, with companies invited to carry out recruitment drives and engage directly with young jobseekers.

Ms Masilagi said organisers deliberately brought together a mix of entrepreneurs, employers and public organisations to make the event more beneficial for young people.

“You know, there’s some youth out there who want to start up a business, but they don’t really feel that encouragement.

“So we’re hoping that seeing them in action tonight, they’d get that encouragement that they need.”

The Fijian Elections Office was also among the organisations participating, with the aim of making information and services more accessible in a setting designed specifically to attract young people.

Ms Masilagi said organisers hope the Youth Skills Market will continue to grow as an annual event, providing a regular platform for youth entrepreneurship, networking and employment opportunities.
